Mr. Speaker, I am not going to enter into any comparison such as that made by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Maclaren) in regard to the importance of the discussion of the Autonomy Bill and compared with the question of freight rates. They are both important in their own way and their own spheres. Nor am X going to dissent from any proposal that may be made in this House having for its object the reduction of freight rates to the shipper, whether he be a farmer or whether he be a manufacturer. Nor, do I complain that the presentation of this case to the House is inopportune, because to my mind it is always opportune to ventilate a grievance here, and the opportuneness can best be measured by the extent of the grievance. But, I wish to call attention to the fact that the proposal now made to the House seems to me to be somewhat irregular, and I want to ascertain whether any good results are likely to flow from it. The object is to lower freight rates. It is generally admitted that ithe freight rates charged by railway companies in many cases are too high, and that there is not a fair rate charged in proportion to the length of the haul. But what do we expect to accomplish by the proposal now before the House ? We had an inquiry made by the Agricultural Committee which appointed a subcommittee to consider that matter, and the report of which subcommittee is transmitted to the House by the main committee. That report contains a schedule of freight rates which it recommends to the House should be sent to the Railway Commission. As I understand it, the duty of a committee of this House under its order of reference, is to secure all necessary data and information and to present its observations and recommendations to parliament. That is done for the purpose of bringing it to the attention of parliament, and in order that the government may take action upon it. Is not the government abandoning its functions when, instead of taking action on the report of a committee of the House, it

merely makes this parliament the medium for transmitting that report to a comparatively irresponsible body. The First Minister shakes his head at that. Let me ask the right lion, gentleman how far can that Railway Commission of its own mere motion, deal with the question we are submitting to it. Will he be good enough to tell me that. There are different classes of freight rates referred to in this report namely, local freight rates, freight rates from certain localities in Canada to a port of shipment for export, and most important of all a reference to the comparatively low freight rates that railway companies are charging on goods collected outside of Canada and hauled through Canada for export or delivery. If I understand correctly the duties of that railway commission it cannot deal with these rates at all.
It can.
In what respect ?

In this respect, that all such tariffs have to be filed with the Railway Commission, and if it were an American railway passing through Canada and carrying goods from an American point to another American point, they cannot carry them through Canada without paying duty unless the tariffs filed by them had first met with the approval of the Railway Commission. If my hon. friend will look at the provisions of the Railway Act, 1903, he will find that pointed out with great particularity.
What section ?
Section 269.

Section 269 reads :
As respects all traffic which shall be carried from any point in a foreign country into Canada, or from a foreign country through Canada into a foreign country by any continuous route owned or operated by any two or more companies, whether Canadian or foreign, a joint tariff for such continuous route shall be duly filed with the board.
That does not deal with the question. It only says that a joint tariff shall be filed ; it provides for what may be done by two railways but this is done by one railway.
And besides there is no provision there with regard to customs duties.

Is there any penalty provided here against the railway companies if they fail to live up to this section ? it must be some other clause because this clause would not apply to the case I have mentioned. I understood from the explanation given by the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) that the Railway Commission was not intended to have the power to deal with through freight rates, and if that be so what is going to be accomplished by referring this report to the Railway Commission ? If the Railway Commission cannot deal with it what are you going to do ? Is it to be assumed by the Railway Commission tnat the schedule of rates contained in this report is stamped with the imprimatur of this House as being correct ? Is this Railway Commission of its own motion to take action on it without any instructions or without any complaint Ijeing made ? I have always understood that the Railway Commission would not take action without complaint being made ; and if that be so it does not appear to me that any good result can come from referring this report to the Railway Commission. I frankly confess that if the Railway Commission of its own motion could take action and force the railway companies to give fair rates, it would be well to have the matter brought before the Railway Commission at the earliest possible moment, but if that be not the case then it is mere child's play to send this report to them. But anyhow it seems to me that this reference amounts to the abandonment by the government of their functions. It is for the benefit of the government that this report of the committee has been submitted to this House, in order that the government may by legislation or otherwise provide a remedy, but under this suggestion we are shifting the responsibility from the government to the Railway Commission, and we are asking the Railway Commission to do what the government should do itself. We know that a grievance exists, and the question is, how shall that grievance be remedied. If by this means a remedy is not brought about, then it is only waste' of time to send the report to the Railway Commission. We can go over these irregular rates as much as we like ; we can quote them in this House and bring them to the attention of the country ; but if no practical good results from it, it is a waste of time.

Some years ago, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce ornamented this House with his person and his eloquence, he promised to have prepared and brought down a statement showing the various rates charged by all the railroads in Canada from centre to centre within Canada, from centres outside of Canada to points in Canada, and from points outside of Canada as well as points in Canada over Canadian roads to foreign ports. I have never yet seen that statement brought down, though it was promised some four years ago. I referred at that time to the question of grain rates, which eh icily interests the part of the country from which I come. Every day through the county which I have the honour to represent, we see passing train loads of grain which is carried from Chicago to the sea-board at the nominal rate of five cents per bushel. That [DOT]grain pays two cents for the water haul to Midland and three cents for the rail haul 1 from Midland to Montreal, whereas the

grain of the Canadian farmers from points along the Midland Railway to the sea-hoard has to pay three and sometimes four times as much as that three cents a bushel. That we have always claimed is a great injustice from the railways which have been built largely by moneys voted by the Canadian municipalities through which they run. I have complained of that again and again. At the time the Act for the creation of the Railway Commission was before this House I drew the attention of the House to the matter, and, if my memory serves me rightly, I was told that it was not intended that the commission should deal with the question of through rates from outside points through Canada over Canadian roads. I have no hesitation in saying that this condition of things is very unfair to the farmers of the Dominion of Canada, especially to the farmers of the province of Ontario, who above any other class in the Dominion have built their own railroads. The county of Victoria has voted hundreds of thousands of dollars to construct railroads in order that the farmers might have competition; but by legislation and amalgamation they have been deprived of competition and now they have to pay extra heavy rates. X maintain that this matter should be dealt with by the government and not referred to the Railway Commission. We do not object to the long haul rate being the same as 'the short haul, but we do object to the short haul rate being greater than the long haul. I trust that the government will take the matter into their consideration and put an end to the present unsatisfactory condition of affairs.

I do not think thei'e is any doubt that the Railway Commission has power to deal with the matters under discussion. The commission already has dealt with the rates for the hauling of cattle from various points in the west to the sea-board. Evidently both the commission and the railway companies realize that they have the power to deal with this question. In many cases the railways discriminate against different sections of the country, and there is no question whatever that the Railway Commission has power to deal with that matter. In regard to the hauling of our live stock, especially to the sea-board, previous speakers have shown that the province of Ontario is very greatly discriminated against. The Michigan farmers have an advantage of at least three cents per hundredweight over the Canadian farmers, and the Grand Trunk railroad .cannot say that it is compelled by competition to give that advantage, because it draws this live	stock from non-competitive
points in Michigan, while it charges our Ontario farmers a flat rate of 25c. per hundredweight, covering a large area extending east to London. The worst feature of these railroad rates is the discrimination which is practiced as between different points in Ontario, -showing that the Mr, SAM. HUGHES.
rates have been devised with a view of getting as much as possible out of the people. For instance, take the article of lumber, which has not been referred to. From Wiar-ton and other northern points as far south as Palmerston the railroads will carry lumber to Montreal for 15c. per cwt. From points further south, such as Woodstock, Iugersoll, London and Simcoe they charge 18c. per cwt. They have a shorter haul and yet they charge three cents per cwt. more. The reason of that is I suppose that the rate was fixed some years ago because. of the water competition that existed from Wiar-ton and points adjacent. The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Maclaren) gave instances of discrimination against the northern districts in favour of more southern districts in regard to the hauling of cement and the handling of cheese products.
So you see the rate is drawn up with a view really of getting as much as they possibly can out of the pockets of the farmers rather than with a view to giving a fair and equitable rate to all portions of the country. These are matters that we feel the Railway Commission should take in hand and deal with firmly and fairly. The railways will no doubt, put up as strong an opposition as they possibly can and they wall employ lawyers competent to handle these questions to go into the matter most thoroughly and most carefully, and the Railway Commission should have all possible information in regard to this question. Let us take for instance, the article of apples which has been referred to. We find that the rate charged on this class of freight for export is far in excess of the rate charged for other commodities of a similar nature. For instance, you have already had given you the figures "of what is charged for the export of grain and grain products ; flour in barrels for export is * charged for at the rate of 13 or 13i cents from the western portions of the province. We find that for apples, a commodity handled in a similar way, carried in barrels, the rate is 231 cents per 100 pounds, fully 30 per cent higher for apples, a commodity of less value although generally the railways fix their rates to some extent in relation to the value of the product. In this case the cheaper commodity is compelled to pay a higher rate by some 30 per cent than the rate charged for grain products. The railways I think are following this course to their own detriment. Last season the rate on apples for export was so high that there was no margin in the English market and thousands and thousands of barrels were allowed to go to waste in the orchards all over the province of Ontario. I am confident from what I know of the situation that fully one-half million barrels of apples were wasted last fall simply because the market prices in England would not pay their handling with the excessive freight rates that prevailed over our

railroads. I lhay say in this connection that while we claim that the rates for export are excessive, these are lower than the rates that prevail for domestic trade, especially for the shipment of goods to points west of Winnipeg. I want to emphasize this point that if the railroads would consider their interests there is no question whatever that they might reduce the rates on apples for export and thereby secure a much larger quantity of freight for export by bringing into the market the fruit that is now going to waste. Three or four years ago a similar condition prevailed when the markets in England were not very good and the excessive freight rates prevented the handling of any large quantities of fruit. I intimated that the rate was lower for export traffic than for local consumption. Your attention has already been called to the fact that the rate to [Montreal from western points is 28 cents per 100 pounds for local consumption, while for export it is 231 cents. We claim that that is too large a difference to be made against freight that is intended for consumption in our own markets. On shipments to any other point east of Montreal or to any other portion of the province a proportionately high rate would prevail as compared with the export rate. I would also call attention to the rate for shipment to Winnipeg. We find that the rate over our railroads is some 90 cents to Winnipeg, while for export to the European markets, London and Liverpool, the rate is only 98 cents and a fraction, and we claim that the rate to Winnipeg is out of proportion to the export rate. Another point to which we would direct the attention of the Railway Commission is the rate that is charged from Winnipeg to all points west of Winnipeg. The railroads give a through rate to Winnipeg but as soon as the goods arrive at Winnipeg, whether it'is apples or any other commodity that is being shipped, the railroads charge a local rate from Winnipeg westward ; they do not give a through rate to any point west of Winnipeg. That to our minds, is a very unfair condition of things. It does not matter whether it is apples, binder twine or agricultural implements, I understand, the same conditions prevail ; they give a through rate to Winnipeg, but a local rate is charged for every article of commerce forwarded to any point west of Winnipeg, and we desire that the attention of the Railway Commission be directed especially to that point. I wish also to refer to a matter touching the internal commerce ' oT the country particularly as touching manufacturing industries. Attention has ibeen called to the fact that rates are given American or foreign shippers sending goods into our own country very much lower rates than the rates that are given to the manufacturer or shipper of goods from points in our own provinces. If a manufacturer of lumber is shipping to Montreal 159
from St. Louis, Cincinnati or Chicago, he is given a very much lower rate over Canadian railways that a shipper of the same commodity living in Canada would receive. Your attention has been drawn to that by the figures presented by the hon. member.for East Kent (Mr. Gordon). I am not going into the figures because they are already before the House, and are there for the information of the commission, but I wish to emphasize this point that in giving a preference to American shippers, Canadian shippers are placed at a great disadvantage in competing against Americans handling a like commodity. Frequently I have had representations made to me from Montreal dealers in lumber that they could not get a rate anything like as favourarble as the rate that would be given to shippers from the cities of the United States. The matter is made very clear when we realize that the rates over our Canadian railroads for persons sending goods into our country from points in the United States are infinitely less than the rates given to any one shipping from one part of our country to another. It is altogether unfair that people living in our own country should be handicapped in this way. You will readily see that our manufacturers are placed at a disadvantage in competing with American manufacturers in regard to agricultural implements or other articles that may be shipped into our country. Reference has already been made to the fact of goods being shipped from Chicago to Toronto at a less rate than they are shipped from Windsor to Toronto or similar points in Canada. It will be seen on examining the figures presented to us that Canadians are discriminated against in this regal'd to an extent of a least 30 to 50 per cent. The elaborate figures that were presented to the House by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gordon) have shown this, and we would desire the commission to have this matter more thoroughly and most carefully inquired into, and we think they should be instructed by this House to deal with this matter firmly and fairly.
We do not wish to treat the railways unjustly. They will put the case as strongly as they can, and, no doubt, will claim that they can not carry Canadian goods as cheaply as they can American goods. But I do not think we should accept this as a reason for subjecting the traffic of Ontario to discrimination. Our railways have been subsidized very heavily, and Ontario, at least the southern portion of it, is thickly peopled and very productive, and we believe that railways are now receiving as large shipments, there area for area, as they receive in their territory on the other side of the line. Hence, if they put forward the argument that they cannot afford to reduce the rates, we shall be prepared to contend that that is not a fair and just argument. When they discriminate against



Canadians as' they do, we think there is strong ground for the contention before the Railway Commission that the rates should be made proportionate to those prevailing on the other side of the line. We know that the Interstate Commerce Act has had a good deal to do with compelling the railroads of the United States to bring their rates to a fair basis. We hope that our commission has the power to deal with this question, perhaps not as effectively as the Interstate Commerce Act provides, but still in a way to secure substantial justice from our railroad companies to those who do business with them. I shall not discuss the matter further, as I believe there are other members who wish to speak upon it. I trust they will emphasize the points already brought before the House. For, Mr. Speaker, this is a very important question. I am inclined to agree with the suggestion that has been made that it would be well if more time were devoted to subjects of this kind rather than so much time to the Autonomy Bill debate. I trust this matter will be dealt with promptly and effectively in the interest of all our producing classes, not only the farmers but the manufacturers as well. And we know that when you reduce rates you increase traffic. Therefore, we believe that our railroads will not suffer in the long run even if they do give us better rates, not merely rates more fairly adjusted, but lower rates for traffic to the sea-board and also, and especially, on goods for local consumption.

I have but few words to say, Mr. Speaker, on the subject, matter of this motion. For the purposes of the motion, I am prepared to concede that the report of the Committee on Agriculture is quite correct and that there are grievances which should be redressed. I shall not discuss that part of the question, as it has been dealt with by other speakers, some of whom at least have had the advantage of being members not only of the Committee on Agriculture but also of the subcommittee whose report has been adopted by the Committee on Agriculture as a whole. No doubt there is a good deal in what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said with regard to the certain difficulties which present themselves in view of the provisions of the Act constituting the Railway Commission. Nevertheless, I think that as to some of the matters at least which are discussed in this report, the Railway Commission would undoubtedly have jurisdiction. Therefore there is no reason why the subject should not engage their attention. But what I particularly wish to suggest to the hon. leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Eaurier) is a point of procedure. It seems to me that the means suggested by this motion for bringing the matter to the at-Mr. M. S. SCHELL,.
tention of the Railway Commission are rather irregular in form. The right hon. gentleman will observe that the report of the committee, after dealing at some length with the questions which have been discussed this afternoon, concludes as follows :
The committee recommend that this report, with the schedules annexed thereto, be referred to the Railway Commission of Canada for the commissioners' consideration and decision forthwith.
And then*the motion which is before the House is that the report be concurred in so far as it recommends the reference of this report to the Railway Commission. We are in this position, therefore, that without having the report of the Committee on Agriculture concurred jn by this House so far as its main features are concerned, we propose to pass a motion that that portion of the report which recommends the reference of the report to the Railway Commission should be concurred in. That seems to me to be rather involved. I should little doubt the propriety, as a matter of parliamentary practice, of referring that report to the Railway Commission even if it had been concurred in by the House. But certainly, until the report as a whole has been concurred in by the House, it seems to me a departure from the ordinary practice to make a motion of this kind. Suppose the report had been concurred in by this House, would it be in accordance with parliamentary usage to suggest that it should be referred to the Railway Commission ? That might be perfectly proper if there is anything in the Railway Act providing that the commission shall take action upon a report of the committee of this House concurred in by the House. I do not profess to be absolutely familiar with the provisions of the Railway Act, but according to my present recollection there is no provision in it which enables the commission to act upon the report of the Committee of Agriculture or any other committee of this House. Therefore, it seems to me, we should do no more by passing this motion than would be accomplished by an hon. member of the House simply inclosing a copy of^the report of the Committee on Agriculture to the Railway Commission in order that they might receive the suggestions therein contained. For, what would be the position ? Evidence has been taken before the Committee on Agriculture. I suppose it will not be suggested by anybody that that evidence could be acted upon by the Railway Commission without giving to the persons who would be affected an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses and to produce evidence on then-own behalf. The result would be that the commission would have to begin the matter de novo. They must act on the initiative of some person or on their own initiative. But there is a method provided in the Railway Act itself by which this matter, having been dealt with by a committee of the

House, could be brought to the attention of the Railway Commission in the ordinary course of procedure. The government in its relation to parliament acts as a committee of parliament. One of the regular standing committees of this House has made a report. That report, when concurred in, would operate as a recommendation by this House to the executive, the government of this country. Under section 45 of the Railway Act, 1903, the government can bring this matter to the attention of the Railway Commission. The following is the provision :
The Governor in Council may at any time refer to the board for a report, or other action, any question, matter, or thing arising, or required to be done, under this Act, or the Special Act, and the board shall without delay comply therewith.
I desire to repeat that I am in entire sympathy with the object of the motion so far as it is designed to bring these matters to the attention of the Railway Commission that it may take such steps as are necessary to redress any grievances that may exist. But I should think the proper course would be to have the report of the. Committee on Agriculture concurred in, if it be the pleasure of the House to concur in it, and then to have the government, under the provision of the Act to which I have referred, require the Railway Commission to investigate this subject and to take such action upon it as may be right in the judgment of the commission with a view to redressing the grievances complained of.

So far as material advantage is concerned, there could be no more important question, I think, brought to the notice of this House, and I am sure the members of the Agricultural Committee are to be congratulated upon the action they have taken. There is no question as to the mode of procedure, in my judgment, i think the committee have acted quite within their powers. They bring to the notice of this House certain grievances, and there is provided by an enactment of this parliament a procedure whereby action shall be taken. In the first place, the Railway Commission can act on its own motion, under the provisions of section 24 of the Railway Act which states :
The board may, of its own motion, or shall, upon the request of the minister, inquire into, hear and determine any matter or thing which, under this Act, it may inquire into, hear and [DOT]determine upon application or complaint, and with respect thereto shall have and may exercise the same powers as, upon any application or complaint, are vested in it by this Act.
There is also section 45 which says :
The Governor in Council may at any time refer to the board for a report, or other action, any question, matter or thing arising, or required to be done, under this Act, or the Spe-159i
cial Act, and the board shall without delay com-plv therewith.
Now certainly a resolution of this House should be taken cognizance of by the government, as well as by the Department of Railways, particularly when it refers to a matter relating to that department. I am sure that if this report is concurred in, and if this resolution is passed, there can be no question as to immediate action being taken, and there are certainly, it is admitted on all sides, grievances to be remedied with respect to these matters. Now the Railway Commission have very full and ample powers to deal with this matter. Reference has been made to the sections referring to tariffs. The board has complete power with respect to all tariffs. They certainly have power with respect to local tariffs ; and all tariffs whether they are joint tariffs, whether they are standard tariffs or local tariffs must be filed with the board, and must meet with the approval of the board, or it may disapprove of them. They can be amended, they can be entirely rescinded, they can be practically swept out of existence, and the board has power to make a new tariff entirely. So far as a continuous route involving a number of railways is concerned, the board have power to apportion to different railways along that route their quota of the entire freight rates from the point of embarkation to tbe point of destination.

Can tbe board compel a railway passing through Canada to post up its freight tariff, its through tariff of rates charged along that railway with regard to freight that does not originate in Canada, but which, originating outsiue of Canada, passes through Canada and is delivered to points outside of Canada V

Unquestionably they can, and I will give the law and the section empowering them to do so. Section 20'.) says :
As respects all traffic which shall he carried from any point in a foreign country into Canada, or from a foreign country through Canada into a foreign country by any continuous route owned or operated by any two or more companies, whether Canadian or foreign, a joint tariff for such continuous route shall he duly filed with the board.
It does not speak of one railway only running continuously.

No, but this is unquestionably with respect to two railways. Where it is one railway simply passing along through a strip of Canadian territory, I do not think there is any provision made, it does not stop, it goes through in bond, it is new traffic in Canada. So far as our neighbours to tbe south of us are concerned, it is simply American traffic coming to the border, running along in bond without ' stoppage, and going again into the United

States. That is a question with which we are not in any way affected, we are not interested.

Has the minister any authority, or has the government any authority, to publish the rates for any kind of traffic originating, say, in Chicago destined for Boston or New York, but passing through Canada over one or more rail- j ways 1

Yes, if it goes over more than one railway, it has, and if the hon. gentleman will refer to section 274 he will find the authority. I have stated that in so far as the freight goes over one railway it simply goes through in bond, and by fiction at least, it is in American territory all the way, it is considered as such.

Will the minister allow me a word ? It may be that the Grand Trunk Railway, although operating as one railway, is owned by a different corporation so far as its line in the United States is concerned, and by another corporation so far as its line in Canada is concerned, although it may come within the provisions of the section as amended.
Mr. EMiMERSON. Under subsection (f) of section 274 it will be seen :
Joint tariffs under section 269 at each freight station or office in Canada to which such tariffs extend.
That is to say, there shall be posted up at every station along the line copies of the tariff. Under section 274 :
The company shall deposit and keep on file in a convenient place open for the inspection of the public, during office hours, a copy of each of its tariffs at the respective places mentioned.
The section goes on to point out where that shall be kept on file, and where it shall be subject to inspection. Now that relates back to section 269, which makes provision with respect to traffic originating in a foreign country and passing through Canada by a different route. Certainly in so far as the Grand Trunk system is concerned, that would comprise two railways. The Grand Trunk Railway having freight originating at Chicago for Portland, for instance, would be obliged to have that tariff posted up at all convenient points named in the Act, they would have to file wtih the Board of Railway Commissioners that joint tariff, and it is subject to approval by the board. Now it seems to me the Act makes every provision for controlling tariffs or railways, whether as respects local freight rates or joint through tariffs.

Do I understand the minister to say that the Railway Commission has power to regulate the rates of the Grand Trunk, not only their freight rates Mr. EMMERSON.
in Canada, but their through rates, for instance, on freights originating in Michigan ?
That is what I state.
I understood there was some difference of opinion.

It is a question of law.
Mr. HAGGAItT. That is under clause 273 in regard to revising the tariffs-1 until such tariff is superseded or disallowed by the board.'

Of course the board has power to do that. If they file a tariff and the board takes no action, then, of course, that tariff has effect, but it is subject to the control of the board and therefore the board can regulate it. If the board takes no action, then, of course, that is a different phase of the question.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Em-merson) one question ? There is a provision in section 268, by means of the imposition of customs duties, for control over the tariffs mentioned in that section. I do not observe any similar provision made for enforcing the tariffs referred to in section 269. Do I make myself clear ?
I see the point.

The hon. minister said that there was some provision of that kind.
Mr. EMMERSuN. My impression was that there was a provision that where freight, en route, passed through Canada originating at a foreign point and destined to a foreign point they were required in that case, unless they complied with the tariff, to pay the customs dues. I was then speaking from memory but on closely reading the clause I find that it provides that :
Any goods carried or being carried from Canada through a foreign country into Canada, in violation of this section, shall, before being admitted into Canada-
Again that would be

be subject to customs duties, as if such
goods were of foreign production and coming into Canada for the first time, and, in case such goods are of a kind which would not otherwise be subject to any customs duties hereunder, shall be subject to a customs duty of 30 per centum of the value thereof.

They cannot do that in the same way, because, if the goods are coming in for consumption they must pay the duties in any case, but could you not make a similar provision by providing that if the tariff was not observed by the railway companies the goods should pay double customs duties or something of that kind ?

There might be a provision made of that kind, I apprehend, and I think there was, speaking simply from memory, hut, there is a remedy even in respect to these companies, and if any one will closely read the several provisions of the Act he will find that the Board of Railway Commissioners have a remedy even as against railways running through Canada with traffic originating in a foreign point and destined to a foreign point of which there are two. Now, this is a question that should be viewed purely from a business standpoint. I do not apprehend that any political aspect can be given to it, and I would be very sorry to see the matter viewed at all from that standpoint. Reference has been made by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) to a combination of railways and he referred to a joint tariff. There Is a provision in this Act whereby a joint through tariff can be arranged and agreed upon by the several railways in Canada, but that tariff must be subject to the approval of the Railway Commission ; that is to say, subject to their supervision and direction. They can control it, they can annul it, and it is entirely under then-direction if they see fit to exercise their powers under this Act.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then I might ask my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals if he thinks it right that they should fix a rate of 6 cents on corn from Chicago to Portland and of 124 cents to Kingston ?

My hon. friend asks me that question. I am not familiar with the tariff from these different points, but I know that my hon. friend has quoted certain tariffs and has stated that the freight rates have been increased. Speaking on the authority of those who have to do with these matters, I stated on a former day in this House, and I now repeat, that freight rates on the Intercolonial have not been increased. I shall take occasion to inquire into the statements made by the hon. gentleman in respect to certain freight rates on the Intercolonial from western points to Fredericton, N.B., as compared with the rates charged over the Canadian Pacific Railway. Certainly the matter has never been brought to my attention and as far as I have any information on the subject at all it is that the rates are uniform, notwithstanding the fact that the Intercolonial Railway has to carry a somewhat greater distance. Combinations of railways can be controlled by the Railway Commission. There cannot be such a thing in Canada as a combination on the part of railways for the simple reason that the commission can annul or rescind the tariff of these railways and they can themselves, in place of the tariff that has been rescinded, originate and create a tariff of their own. They can also say as to what proportion shall go to this railway and what
proportion shall go to that. They have the right to determine as to the total freight rate from the point of shipment to the point of destination, and as well they have the right to determine as to the apportionment of the total among the different lines of railway over which the traffic may be hauled. My hon. friend cited an instance and gave figures as to certain charges from Sydney to Brockville and he also quoted certain freight rates from Brockville to Pittsburg. Pennsylvania.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Brockville to Gananoque.
It is immaterial- Brockville to Gananoque.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, it is not immaterial. The rate from Sydney to Brockville is 25 cents and from Brockville to Gananoque, a distance of thirty miles, 124 cents is added to that.

You there get the local rate and it is governed by the want of competition. But, my hon. friend said that he could ship from Brockville to Pittsburg at a very much less rate. Unquestionably. The distance from Brockville to Pittsburg is less than 600 miles while the distance from Brockville to Sydney is, I think, 1,036 miles. By the longest route, the Buffalo, Rochester and Pittsburg road, the distance to Pittsburg is 598 miles. There is a more direct route than that. That is a round about route by way of Rochester passing through Bradford and Alleghany city to Pittsburg. So you have a haulage of 1,036 miles on the one hand as against a haulage of 598 miles on the other. It would be idle to compare rates when there is such a discrepancy as to distance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
What I complain most of is hauling it over 1,000 miles for 25 cents and then hauling the same car without unloading thirty miles further and then charging 12* cents.
Mr. EMMKIbON. That is by reason of the local raw

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then why should the Railway Commission allow such a local rate ?

I do not know that the matter has been brought to the notice of the Railway Commission. Let me say this on behalf of the Railway Commission, that they certainly have, taking into consideration the conditions under which they have worked since their organization, gotten through with a tremendous amount of work. I think I brought to the notice of the House on a former occasion the number of orders which the Railway Commission had passed, ex parte orders in the main-at least the major portion of them were ex parte orders -but a very large portion of them were contested cases. The contested cases have, I think, exceeded 100; the uncontested cases were away up in the hundreds ; and

if I mistake not, and I speak subject to correction, the number of orders issued was in the vicinity of 800. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says that in the Railway Act he finds provision for protecting the railways against fraud and dishonesty, but that nowhere in the Act is there protection for the shipper. The cases are not at all analogous. The shipper has his remedy in law against the railway company, just the same as any person doing business has his remedy against the party with whom he deals. The provisions in the Railway Act against fraud and dishonesty in classification and weight are placed there largely to avoid the necessity of having goods held up at certain points to be subject to thorough investigation by the officers of the company and to prevent the delays that would ensue. The railway companies are common carriers subject to the common law, and, having certain responsibilities upon them, they have a right in the public interest to be protected. It is the same protection that has been accorded them for years, and it is the same protection that is accorded to them in all countries.

What has all this to do with lowering the freight rates ? The complaint is that the farmers of this country are charged unfair rates and are not properly protected, and it appears to me that a shipper might be protected when a farmer would not be protected at all. As I understood the minister, he said the farmers had nothing to do with it, but I can tell him that it is the farmer that has to pay the freight rates in the end. If the Minister of Railways is a farmer in Michigan and I am a farmer in Canada, and he can send his produce through Canada to Portland or Boston at a less rate than I can send my products to Montreal, then I am at a disadvantage and cannot compete with him. The consumer is not affected and the shipper is not affected, but it is the farmer who is injured in trying to get his goods to the foreign market.

I am not disputing the position taken by my hon. friend, but we were discussing the carriage of freight through Canada to the sea-board on a continuous line of railway ; and if the shipper is not affected, then my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) will have to settle the question with my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor).
The member for Leeds or the member for East Northumberland cannot settle it, but the .Minister of Railways can, and the blame is on him if he does not settle it.
I am afraid my hon. friend is unduly absolving himself from responsibility.
Well, 1 will change places with you and take the responsibility, and settle it, too.

My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) has a certain amount of responsibility as a representative of the people, and he cannot unload it on to my shoulders or on to the shoulders of the member for Leeds. The hon. member for Leeds raised the question, and I do not say he improperly raised it, as to the distinction between the railways and the shippers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I referred to the fact that the railway companies have notified the shippers that if they give improper weights or classification they will be subject to penalties under the Railway Act. The railway companies can protect themselves, for they have the classification and they have the scales to weigh the goods. The Minister of Railways says that the receiver of goods from a railway company can protect himself by law, but how can he ? Two years ago I received from Tennessee a carload of rims stripped, and when we weighed it it was
5,000	pounds short. I put in a claim to the railway company for a drawback, but they said it had been weighed on some railway connection in the United States and they refused to pay. Two or three months ago a carload came to us, and I know there were several thousand pounds short, and although we were badly in need of the goods we had to dicker with the railway company for several months, and finally they said : Put on a man and we will put on a man and settle the matter, and when that was done it was found to be 10,000 pounds short. If I had paid that money, how could I collect from a railway company away down in Tennessee ? I would bring a man forward to swear that the weights were not correct, and they would bring a man to swear that the weights were correct. I have claims standing for four or five years against railway companies, and I cannot get them paid. It is the shippers who need protection, and not the railway companies.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) purchased a ton of hay from a neighbour and sent his team to get it, and it was afterwards found that there were only 1,740 pounds in it instead of 2,240, he would have his remedy against the vendor.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That man is in Canada.

So he is ; and the railway company, to whom he paid his money, is in Canada. If by misrepresentation or mistake he is called on to pay more money than he rightly should, he has eertain-1.' a remedy against the party to whom he paid that money. My hon. friend says that one man would swear one thing and another man would swear another thing. The point is :	Is there less weight ? If
there is, that is capable of being demonstrated, and my hon. friend would have his remedy, as people have their remedies in all walks of life and all business transactions occurring daily throughout the country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But the railway company have the power within their own hands tc make the right classification and to make the weight right before they deliver the goods. They can collect the money as they go along.

But my hon. friend forgets that they can only make that classification in accordance with the statute. It can only be done with the approval of a tribunal appointed by the parliament of Canada, namely, the Railway Commission.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But why does the parliament of Canada put a penalty on the shipper who sends out a box of goods marked as weighing 200 pounds that weighs only 150 pounds, when the railway company has the power to fix the right weight ?

The penalty is fixed, not for misunderstanding, but for wilful fraud. That is an element that has to be taken into consideration, and the penalty is enforcible only under these conditions. It is true, there may be some error in respect of weight, but that can be remedied, as it always is remedied when it is demonstrated between individuals. I need not speak further with respect to the matter. We must all bear in mind that so far as Canada is concerned, indeed, so far as this continent is concerned, the Act of 1903, is practically experimental. It was,
I think, very wisely drawn. It is not a perfect Act; we do not have such even in this twentieth century ; but we are enjoying it as an experiment at least, and, in so far as the results are concerned, if general observations and the testimony of people who have had some experience of the operations of the commission are of any value, it has been productive of much good it the people of Canada. The questions they have decided with respect to level crossings and other crossings, with respect to disputes between railways and between shippers and railway companies-all these things go to. show that the Act has been of material advantage to the people of Canada, even though it has been in operation only a few months, although probably two or three years would demonstrate more clearly its advantages. IV e should not forget that in the light of experience we can act; and, if the provisions of this Act do not meet the conditions in Canada to-day, it is with-'n the power of this parliament to make the necessary amendments covering all these difficulties, and remedying the grievances which may exist.

McIvENZIE. I may say that when the subcommittee took this matter up and looked into it, they very soon became convinced that it was impossible for them to furnish the information covering the whole country in the short space of time allotted to them. In speaking to the motion, I said that the Railway Commission were dealing with this matter, and while they were doing so we wanted to give them our evidence. We therefore thought it advisable to take some special farm products in Ontario as examples, and with that we left it. Cement was spoken of by Mr. Maclaren, who was interested in it, and being on the committee was allowed special license in regard to it.

Of course that may be the exact reading of it, but it does not seem to me that this is the case we want to get at, the question whether a road is operated by two companies or one. The question to which I wish to get a reply is:	Can the
Railway Commission compel one or two companies, as the case may be, which handle goods collected in the United States and which pass through Canada to another point in the United States, upon which a lower freight rate is charged than the same company exacts on goods collected in Canada and conveyed to that same point, to reduce their freight rates to the same proportionate rate as is charged on the same class of goods collected in American territory.

I cannot say that the commission has power to deal with a rate on freight from an American point to another American point even if it passes through Canada. I am not prepared to say that, but I have no doubt that the commission can take that rate of freight into its consideration when it authorizes a rate in Canada and can regulate its rate in Canada in accordance with justice by comparing the rate with that charged from one American point to another. I think in that way the commission has absolute power over the rates from any Canadian point to any point elsewhere and therefore it has practical power to deal with rates from Canadian points to outside points in comparison with or in relation to the rates from points in the United States to other points in the United States. To that extent I have no doubt whatever that they have the whole power and I think that answers the objection which the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) seems to take.

That answers the objection fully, because if I understand correctly in the schedule of rates that was given many of these quotations referred to freight collected in the west and carried through Canada consigned to points in the United

States in the east, and as I understood the explanation of the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) when this Bill was under discussion, we could not deal with or control through freight rates. Believing that, it seems to me this could not be worked out, but if the commission has the power to deal with it it can be worked out.

What the ex-Minister of Railways no doubt meant was that the commission had no power to control rates from one point in the United States to anther point in the United States, in which he was correct, but when dealing with a rate from one Canadian point to another the commission has the power and it may utilize its knowledge of the American rates in regulating the rate to another Canadian point and therefore the knowledge of these facts which under the Act the railway company is obliged to supply to the commission if it passes through Canada is useful as a guide and help in regulating or deciding the rate from a point in Canada to another point in Canada or to a point outside of Canada. My hou. friend will see that the Railway Commission has absolute control over all freight rates in Canada; it can authorize a tariff or change of tariff or fix a tariff, and if it finds at any time that circumstances and conditions have changed and that any tariff is no longer working justly it may then cancel that tariff and substitute another. It has, therefore, I think absolute and complete control over a tariff of rates in Canada. But I would like to point out that the Railway Commission is composed of men. The Railway Commission can only do a certain amount of work within a certain period of time. The Railway Commission, to my personal knowledge, has been working extremely hard on its work and an enormous number of questions have been submitted to it. It has had to deal for the 'first time in the history of Canada with an enormous mass of tariff questions, of railway freight questions, and I had myself no conception until it was brought to my attention of the immense complication of tariff rates and of the enormous difficulty there is in dealing justly and fairly with them. It is a very intricate question, so intricate that it has been found necessary by the great railway companies to appoint special agents, men of special qualifications, men who are difficult to find and who, when found, must be paid the highest salaries of any men employed by a railway company, with the exception possibly of the president. It is a very complicated question and it is impossible that the Railway Commsision at one blow or in a few months could overcome the difficulties of this work and establish an absolutely fair set of rates all through the country at one fell swoop. It will take time.
I was not making complaint with regard to the time.

I do not say that my hon. friend was complaining. But I point this
out in justice to the Railway Commission and to the House. The Railway Commission have not to deal with the freight rates alone. They have to deal with difficulties that have arisen between municipalities or corporations and the railways, with difficulties that have arisen among the railways themselves concerning conflicting interests and conflicting claims. And while, the freight rate question should be dealt with in the interest of the public and is probably the most important question which will come before the Railway Commission; there are other questions which the members of the commission cannot ignore but which they must deal with. I think the members of the Committee on Agriculture are to be congratulated on bringing this question in this way before the House and preparing for the reference of it to the Railway Commission. I am satisfied that the Railway Commission will take the matter up and deal with it as promptly as possible, and I think that the form in which it is put before the House will accomplish the object in view, which is so important in the interest of the farmers. I may say, in regard to that, that while the committee has been dealing simply with one phase of this question as affecting particularly western Ontario, there is no doubt that there are questions of a similar character affecting other parts of the country ; and I think it would be well for the Committee on Agriculture, on a future occasion, perhaps at another session, if it is not possible to take it up this session, to take up other branches of this question and deal with them in the same way as in this case. I would say in this respect that the eastern parts of Canada also suffer from discrimination and difficulties in regard to freight rates, perhaps, just as greatly as the farmers of western Ontario, though we do not happen to have exactly the same relationship towards the farmers of the United States that the farmers of western Ontario have. These things are work for the future, and I hope they will be taken up and dealt with in the same manner as in this case.

I would like to ask if the Railway Commission have power to deal with the rates in a case where a steamship company and a railway company combine to give the rate. I have known cases in which the rate from Liverpool through to Brantford or London has been less than from Montreal to the same points, the rate for the short haul being actually greater than for the long haul. Have the commission power to deal with such a case ?

I desire to say a few words to the House on this very im-

portant question regarding discrimination in freight rates. It has been suggested by the chairman of the committee that the scope of this report should be confined principally to one province. I think to do so would be to take a very narrow view of the transportation question in Canada. You will agree with me, I think, Mr. Speaker, that it concerns more than one province, and that while discriminations and anomalies may exist in freight rates all over Ontario, they exist equally in other sections of this great Dominion. Those gentlemen who are suffering from these grievances have my sympathy, as I am sure they have the sympathy of every well wisher of Canada. But I wish to point out, and I would be remiss in my duty if I tailed to point out to this House that in the maritime provinces, and especially in my own province of Prince Edward Island, there are anomalies and discriininaations in railway rates much heavier and more disadvantageous than any which have been referred to yet. I will mention only one or two items at present, as probably this question will come up again and be discussed more fully at another time. Borne reference has been made to freight rates on cattle. Now I would like to point out that a carload of cattle, say twenty head, can be taken from Guelph, Ontario, and landed in Halifax for the -sum of $65, that is a distance of over 1,000 miles. But down in Prince Edward Island, to take a car of cattle from a point on the Prince Edward Island Railway to Halifax will cost $70, and the distance is less than 200 "u'ies. When a farmer in Prince Edward Island wants to ship a car of cattle to Truro, or or even to Pictou, from some points on the Prince Edward Island Railway he has to pay as high as $05. Reference lias also been made to the discriminations in freight rates on grain, and I will give an instance in that line also. At present you can take a car of grain 1,300 miles west of Nova Scotia down to Pictou, a car containing
2.000	bushels, and it will cost you $142, or a little over a third of a cent a ton per mile. But in my own itrovince, if you want to -send the same quantity of grain,
2.000	bushels of oats from a point on the Prince Edward Island Railway either to Truro or Halifax, you have to pay $100 in winter and $S0 in summer. So that, whereas you can get a carload of grain carried over 1,000 miles from the west to the maritime provinces for $142, in the province I have the honour to come from you have to pay $80 for carrying it 200 miles. I could multiply instances of the same character. In fact every thing as a province we have to ship, but I call the attention of the chairman of the committee to these instances only, with the hope that he will not confine the scope of this investigation to one province. I trust that when these discrim-

inations that have been mentioned by other speakers are referred to the Railway Commission, it will also take into account anomalies which exist in regard to all the other provinces, east and west, from British Columbia to Prince Edward Island. I think those two instances alone will satisfy any lion, member that they require the attention of the Railway Commission with a view to remedying the grievances which they indicate. It was not at first my intention to speak on this subject, but when I heard several lion, members mention -the discrimination which they declared to be burdensome in their provinces, I could not help refering to much more serious grievances in my own province. I think, Sir, that this is a very important subject, and I agree with the remark that it is of equal importance to the subject of separate schools which this House has been discussing for five or six weeks. I hope this government wil lake up this question seriously, with a view of remedying the grievances complained of.

Before this discussion closes, I would like to say a few words on the same line as the hon. member who has just preceded me (Mr. A. Martin). When this matter was taken up before the Agriculture Committee it covered the subject of freight rates over the whole Dominion. To facilitate the work of the committee, a subcommittee was appointed, who took up the question of freight rates confining it practically to Ontario. When their report was presented I took exception to it, because I knew that discriminations existed in the other provinces. I was met with the statement that the work of the committee was only to establish that discriminations existed by getting some evidence. Then, when the matter came before the House it would establish that discriminations existed and when the evidence went before the commission we would all have a chance from our various provinces of presenting evidence. I am anxious that this matter be looked into from the position of the province of Quebec. I have been waiting for somebody better qualified to speak in regard to the province of Quebec than I am, but as nobody has done so I wish to bring up a case that we have been complaining of. I will give an instance which exists in my own county. From the village of Hemmingford to the city of Montreal the distance is forty-four miles. The rate charged on a carload of apples is forty dollars. I have letters from people in that vicinity complaining very much about it. As my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) said this afternoon probably we do not appreciate the effect of American competition as they do in the west, but what we object to is the discrimination of our own railways. It exists in this way that from any place that is near the

water front where there is competition with the boats, the rates are much more favourable than they are from a place such as I have mentioned where it is impossible to get competition. The freight must go by the Grand Trunk Railway ; consequently, there is discrimination in rates. Before this goes before the Railway Commission I would like it to be stated and understood that this discrimination extends all over Canada so that when we present our evidence to the commission we may have a resolution backing us up. We are willing to present our evidence but we do not want it stated to the commissioners that this House considers that discrimination in rates exists only in the province of Ontario. We want it understood that it exists all over so that we may have an opportunity of presenting our evidence.

Mr. Speaker, I think the subject now before the House is one worthy of the attention of every member of this House. The hon. member for Queen's, P.E.I. (Mr. Martin) has complained, as have some other hon. gentlemen, that attention has been given exclusively to the matter of freight rates as it concerns the province of Ontario. I am sure that it was not the intention of the special committee appointed by the Committee on Agriculture to give particular attention to this matter in one province more than in another, but it was felt that some report had to be brought in, and brought in quickly, to be of any use for the purpose of the Railway Commission. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), in his address, spoke in rather a complaining way because the Railway Commission had not acted very quickly and applied remedies before this. I do not think the Railway Commission is deserving of censure or blame in this matter, I do not think that the people of this country, I do not think that the farmers of this country, have the idea or the desire that the Railway Commission shall be used simply as a means of attack upon the railway companies. I do not think that we desire to have any treatment from the railway companies beyond that which is reasonable and fair. We ask that they shall accord us as shippers of freight treatment that is reasonable and right, and we are willing to accord to the railway companies in return treatment that is right and equitable, as far as they are concerned. In order to arrive at a conclusion as to what is right and just and fair, a great deal of evidence will have to be obtained. This evidence will have to come from a large area. Evidence will have to be heard from many persons, and evidence will have to be heard for and against. This will take time and occasion delays. We not only desire to do what is right and fair to all concerned, but we realize that if this parliament, or if the Railway Commission, should impose unreasonable burdens upon the railway companies, or if they
should restrict or interfere with the business of the railway companies, or reduce their freight rates so that their income, with reasonable management and proper economy, would not yield a reasonable return upon the money invested, the result would be, not only disastrous to the interests of the railway companies, but disastrous to the best interests of the people of this country. Therefore, we only desire and expect and ask for treatment that shall be fair and right. It may be thought by some that a matter of freight that can only make a difference in the price of a bushel of grain of probably a cent, or a fraction of a cent in the price of a pound of beef, is, after all, a very trifling matter, but we must remember that the farmer is a manufacturer, that there is a cost price upon every article that he manufactures or sends to market. We must remember that the farmer supports his family, carries on his business and pays his debts, not from the gross price of the articles or commodities that he sells, but from the narrow margin that he may look upon as profit, as part of the price that is over and above the cost of that production, and on one cent a bushel, or a fraction of a cent per pound in the price of the beef cattle that he sells, or the price of his land or dairy products, forms a very large proportion of the margin of profit. I believe, Sir, that our farmers are -equal in intelligence, and equal in so far as their habits of industry, economy and thrift are concerned, to the farmers of any other part of this globe; but I do believe that if they are handicapped by unfair and unreasonable freight charges, it will be the duty of every member of this House to lend whatever assistance he can, and to use whatever influence he may possess in any reasonable way to remove that handicap, and place our farmers upon an equal footing with the farmers in the country to the south of us. As a further evidence, if further evidence be required, of the lack of method or system, and I think I may say lack of fairness, in imposing freight rates, I might read a letter, dated the 25th of this month, and addressed to the hon. member for South Bruce (Mr. McKenzie). The hon. member for South Bruce had intended reading this letter when he spoke upon this subject, but inadvertently omitted to do so. *The letter is addressed by Mr. John Toliuie, of the Ontario People's Salt and Soda Company of Kincardine, and is as follows :-
Kincardine, Ont., 25th April, 1905. Peter McKgnzie, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa.
My Dear Sir,-Last week we shipped a car of salt to William Simpson, Ridgetown. The usual rate was five cents per hundred pounds on the Grand Trunk Railway to St. Thomas and two cents per hundred pounds on the Michigan Central Railway from St. Thomas to Ridgetown, and while the Grand Trunk Railway only charges the five cents as formerly the Michigan Central Railway charged six cents per hundred

pounds, making a total of eleven cents against seven cents, the former rate. Thus the Grand Trunk Railway carried this freight 116 miles for five cents iper hundred pounds, and the [DOT]Michigan Central Railway charged six cents for 44 miles. Would you he kind enough to draw the attention of the House to this state of affairs, and also to one of the members of the Railway Commission and greatly oblige.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) JOHN TOLMIE,
Secretary.
